text:
The Chinese see the hour in cats’ eyes. One day, a missionary walking through a suburb of Nanking noticed that he had forgotten his watch and asked a little boy what time it was.

The child of the Celestial Empire hesitated at first; then, collecting himself, he answered: “I shall tell you.” A few moments later he reappeared carrying a large cat, and, looking into what is commonly called the whites of its eyes, declared without hesitation: “It is not yet exactly noon.” And so it was.

As for me, if I lean toward the beautiful feline, so aptly named, who is at once an honor to her sex, the pride of my heart, and the perfume of my spirit, whether by night or day, in light or opaque shadow, in the depths of her adorable eyes I always see the hour clearly, always the same: an hour vast, solemn, immense as space, without divisions of minutes or seconds, a motionless hour unmarked by clocks, and yet light as a sigh, swift as a glance.

If some tiresome person came to disturb me while my gaze rested on so delicious a sphere; if some evil and intolerant spirit, some Demon of untimeliness, came to say: “What are you looking at so carefully? What do you seek in that creature’s eyes? Do you see the hour there, prodigal and idle mortal?” I would answer without hesitation: “Yes, I see the hour in them. It is Eternity!”

Is it not true, madam, that this is a truly meritorious madrigal and as emphatic as you yourself? Indeed, I have taken so much pleasure in embroidering this presumptuous gallantry that I shall ask nothing of you in return.

translation.title: The Clock
translation.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire. The prose-poem structure, Nanking anecdote, and mock-gallant conclusion are retained.
